title: Knowledge starts with humility
hookLine: Arjuna argues like an expert, then says: teach me. The Gita's list of knowledge starts there.
tomorrow: The same Lord in all beings
last: KSHETRA: THE BODY IS THE FIELD; YOU'RE ITS KNOWER.

cards: At the start of the Gita, Arjuna argues like an expert. He's a great archer and a prince, and he lays out the case against this war: family will be destroyed, the old ways will fall, it's wrong to kill your own teachers.
Then, a few verses into chapter two, he stops. He admits his mind is confused about what's right. And he says to Krishna: I am your student.
I've taken refuge in you. Teach me. That's the moment the Gita really begins.
Not when Arjuna knows the most, but when he admits he doesn't.

teach.b: Chapter thirteen turns that moment into a list. Verse seven. Krishna gives a heading, knowledge, and the first word under it is amanitva: humility, not thinking much of yourself.
Then adambhitva, no pretending. Then ahimsa, doing no harm. Then patience, straightforwardness, serving your teacher, cleanliness, steadiness, self-control.
In many Hindu homes that line still lives in the body: you bow, or touch an elder's feet, before you learn from them. The list keeps going. Not being dragged by the senses.
Not being ruled by the sense of I. Not clinging too tightly to home and family. Staying even when things go well and when they don't.
Steady devotion. A taste for quiet places. Then the surprise.
This, Krishna says, is called knowledge, and whatever is its opposite is ajnana, ignorance.
So in the Gita, knowledge isn't only what's in your head; it's how you live. A brilliant, arrogant person, by this definition, is missing the first item.
From verse twelve the chapter turns to what is to be known, Brahman, and the words go strange on purpose. It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes and faces everywhere.
It's far away, and it's near, inside beings and outside them. Verse seventeen calls it the light of lights, beyond darkness.
And the door to it starts where Arjuna started: humility.

how: Hindu teachers often quote Gita 13.7–13.11 as a checklist of character for students, starting with amanitva, humility; many traditions treat serving and honoring the teacher as part of this knowledge.

o: honesty, never telling a single lie
respect, giving honor to all elders
humility, not thinking much of yourself

games.q: what's on the list of knowledge — tap the pairs.

s: the Gita's list of 'knowledge' is mostly facts and doctrines
it's mostly qualities of character: humility, patience, steadiness, no harm.
the first word on the list is humility
amanitva: not thinking much of yourself.
verse 17 calls what is to be known the light of lights
the light of lights, beyond darkness.

games.q: Arjuna has argued against the war like an expert. what turns the argument into the Gita?
o: he admits he's confused and asks Krishna to teach him.
Krishna orders him to stop talking.
games.why: Gita 2.7: i am your student; teach me. humility opens the door, and chapter 13 puts it first on the list of knowledge.

practice: Think of a recent moment you needed to be right, a text thread, a meeting, a family dinner, and just see it. Replay it with the need dropped one notch: ask a question instead of making a point. Then do what Arjuna did.
If you pray, bow your head and ask God, teach me. If you don't, say it inwardly to the day ahead: i don't know everything yet. Notice how that softer version feels in the chest.

wordCard.voice: Amanitva, humility, not thinking much of yourself. Gita thirteen, seven: the first word on the list Krishna calls knowledge; its opposite is ignorance.

orig.note: Sanskrit: amanitva, humility, literally not-being-proud; the first item in Gita 13's list of knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: amanitva: knowledge begins with humility. Arjuna's did: teach me. Day two hundred five, done.
